bundle.prompt:
Below is a passage from a college course, the course plan for its chapter (objectives and concepts, by id), and the plan items the passage is declared to teach.
For each declared item, say whether the passage teaches or practises it ("yes"), touches it only in passing ("passing"), or does not deal with it ("no").
If the passage teaches an item of the plan it is not declared for, name its id. If it teaches nothing in the plan at all, say so.
Judge what the passage does for a student, not its wording or quality.
Reply with JSON only, exactly this shape: {"nonce": "9681b9fc2ce75025", "links": [{"id": "...", "verdict": "yes" | "passing" | "no", "why": "..."}], "also": ["<id>"], "offPlan": false}

THE CHAPTER'S PLAN
- objective.le-chatelier.state-principle: State Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium that is disturbed shifts to a new equilibrium that partially counteracts the disturbance.
- objective.le-chatelier.predict-concentration-shift: Predict the direction an equilibrium shifts when the concentration of a reactant or product is increased or decreased.
- objective.le-chatelier.predict-temperature-shift: Predict the direction an equilibrium shifts when the temperature changes, by treating heat as a reactant for an endothermic reaction or a product for an exothermic one.
- objective.le-chatelier.predict-pressure-shift: Predict the effect of a volume or pressure change on a gas-phase equilibrium by comparing the moles of gas on each side of the equation.
- objective.le-chatelier.explain-inert-and-catalyst: Explain why adding an inert gas at constant volume, and why adding a catalyst, do not shift the equilibrium.
- concept.le-chatelier.principle-statement: Le Chatelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium disturbed by a change in a determining factor adjusts to a new equilibrium that partially counteracts the change.
- concept.le-chatelier.concentration-shift: Increasing the concentration of a species shifts the equilibrium toward the opposite side to consume the added species, and decreasing it shifts toward that side to replace it.
- concept.le-chatelier.heat-as-species: A temperature change is handled by treating heat as a product for an exothermic reaction and as a reactant for an endothermic reaction, then applying the same reasoning as for a concentration change.
- concept.le-chatelier.temperature-changes-k: A temperature change is unique in that it changes the value of the equilibrium constant, whereas concentration and pressure changes do not.
- concept.le-chatelier.volume-pressure-shift: For a gas-phase equilibrium, decreasing the volume (raising the pressure) shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas, and increasing the volume shifts it toward the side with more moles of gas.
- concept.le-chatelier.inert-gas-no-shift: Adding an inert gas at constant volume changes no partial pressure and therefore does not shift a gas-phase equilibrium.
- concept.le-chatelier.catalyst-no-shift: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor and therefore does not change the position or composition of the equilibrium.
- misconception.le-chatelier.cancels-disturbance: Le Chatelier's principle lets the system completely cancel the disturbance and return to its original equilibrium.
- misconception.le-chatelier.catalyst-increases-product: Adding a catalyst increases the amount of product present at equilibrium.
- misconception.le-chatelier.inert-gas-shifts: Adding an inert gas at constant volume shifts a gas-phase equilibrium because the total pressure rises.
- misconception.le-chatelier.heat-raises-yield: Raising the temperature always increases the yield of product.
- misconception.le-chatelier.pressure-shifts-every: A pressure change shifts every gas-phase equilibrium, even one with equal moles of gas on both sides.
- concept.course.dynamic-equilibrium: A reversible reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal, nonzero rates.
- concept.course.equilibrium-constant: The equilibrium constant quantifies the balance of products to reactants once a reaction has reached equilibrium.
- concept.course.q-versus-k: Comparing the reaction quotient to the equilibrium constant predicts the direction in which a reaction not yet at equilibrium will move.
- concept.course.le-chatelier-principle: Le Chatelier's principle predicts qualitatively how an equilibrium already reached shifts to partially counteract a disturbance.
- concept.course.temperature-changes-k: A temperature change both shifts the equilibrium position and changes the value of the equilibrium constant, whereas concentration, volume, and pressure changes shift the position without changing the equilibrium constant.

DECLARED ITEMS
- objective.le-chatelier.predict-concentration-shift

TEXT BEFORE THE PASSAGE (context only)
Justify the answer to Q3 using $Q_r$ and $K$ instead of Le Chatelier's principle. *(Objective 2)*

PASSAGE (Answer 5)
Adding $\ce{H2}$ increases the denominator of the quotient, so $Q_r$ falls below $K$. Since
$Q_r < K$, the reaction shifts forward until $Q_r$ rises back to $K$. Note that $K$ itself is
unchanged: only the composition moved.
